newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke says no need for tax rises in budget.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke says no need for tax rises in budget.

text.p: Former British Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke said on Friday there was no need for his successor, Labour's Gordon Brown, to raise taxes in his first budget next week.

In a budget preview on Sky Television, Clarke, who has returned to the parliamentary backbenches after being defeated by William Hague in the contest for the Conservative leadership, also suggested that Brown had been doctoring some forecasts.
"Gordon Brown has been altering some of the forecasts to create the impression that borrowing is not coming down fast enough and that he needs to raise tax," Clarke said.
"Borrowing is coming down at a satisfactory rate...My opinion is that this budget is unnecessary."

Many economists expect Brown to try to rein in soaring consumer spending by raising taxes in his July 2 budget, although some believe any fiscal tightening will be targeted at the corporate sector rather than the personal sector.

Clarke said there was no need to put up taxes when the Bank of England, which was empowered by Brown to set interest rates, could act to prevent any resurgence in inflation by tightening monetary policy.

Official interest rates have been raised twice in the past two months to their present 6.5 percent level. The Bank of England's new monetary policy committee will hold its next meeting on July 9 and 10, a week after budget day.
Clarke said Brown aimed to raise taxes so that he would have money set aside to win favour with voters closer to the next election, due in five years' time.
"In my opinion, this is inventing an excuse to raise revenue which he will spend in politically popular ways towards the last years of this parliament.

"It's also an attempt to raise fears about the direction of borrowing and set himself some easier targets, so that he can claim in future years that he is doing well when borrowing falls faster than the new forecast."

Brown has said that the centrepiece of his first budget will be a "welfare-to-work" programme to create jobs for 250,000 young people, financed by a "windfall" tax on the profits of privatised utility firms.

The Labour party, anxious to shake off the "tax-and-spend" image that helped to keep it in opposition for 18 years, promised before the May 1 election not to raise income tax rates and to live within tight public spending limits laid down by Clarke for two years.
In reference to Brown's ambition to be an "iron chancellor", Clarke said: "I think we'll find that Gordon Brown has put too much iron into his chancellorship too quickly."
"He was elected promising faster growth and quicker falls in unemployment," Clarke added. "In two years time we will find that he has slowed down growth, and we have slower falls in unemployment."
